head:
Seniors · Training

Ageing while training: what masters athletes show

With age, breathing capacity, muscle and speed decline. Nobody escapes this, not even people who have trained for thirty years. The real question lies elsewhere: does what you do change how fast that decline happens, and if so, by how much, and until when is it still time to act? This article follows the evidence step by step, from the broadest picture to the most precise, before answering.

The question

You are 45, 55 or 65, and you train or are thinking of starting. Around you, you see people your age who climb stairs without thinking about it, and others who stop halfway up. You hear that “it all depends on genes”, or that “it's age, whatever you do”. So you wonder what effort is for: does it really slow anything down, or are you just watching more closely a slope that is the same for everyone?

A second doubt comes quickly. People who are fit at 70 may already have been fit at 40, and would have stayed fit whatever they did. If so, training has nothing to do with it, and you can spare yourself the effort. So there are two nested questions: a question of fact (does the slope change?) and a question of cause (is it training that changes it?).

So-called “masters” athletes, adults who train and compete in age categories, are a good field for answering this: they train for a long time, they are measured often, and they can be compared with those who have slowed down. This is not enough to conclude, and the article will say why.

The question

As we age, does training really change how fast we lose endurance, muscle and speed, and what can be done in practice at your age?

What is at stake

This is not about records. Three things are at stake: your independence, your safety and your lifespan.

Independence. A Canadian researcher, R. J. Shephard, reviewed the question in the British Journal of Sports Medicine. His reading: loss of independence becomes likely when maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max, the reference measure of endurance) falls to around 18 mL/kg/min in men and 15 in women, a threshold that would be reached around 80 to 85 years of age. The closer you get to it, the higher the share of your maximum that everyday tasks (climbing a flight of stairs, carrying shopping) demand. He adds that regular aerobic exercise could push this threshold back by ten years or more, and specifies that the weight of this factor remains to be clarified.15

Muscle and safety. According to a popular-science summary from Harvard Medical School, muscle loss starts between 30 and 40, becomes visible around 60, and a 30-year-old man can expect to lose about 25% of his muscle mass and muscular strength by 70.14 The number on the scale barely moves, because fat replaces muscle, which makes the loss discreet until the day it gets in the way. As for falls, the World Health Organization states that balance and functional strength exercises reduce them, with a high level of evidence.8

Lifespan. Among the people aged 85 and over in the Newcastle 85+ cohort (845 people followed for 5.35 years on average), each extra kilo of grip strength at baseline goes with a risk of death about 5% lower (risk ratio 0.95). This link is an association: the authors themselves see it mainly as a reflection of physical reserves, not as a demonstrated effect of strength on survival.16

That is why the question cannot be left unanswered. A slope of decline that varies by a factor of two, repeated over thirty or forty years, does not produce the same person at the end. If training acts on this slope, not knowing it costs you years of independence; if it does not, you need to know that too. We start with the widest picture.

Step 1 of 6 · The whole population
rest:
Everyone declines, athletes included

The claim: decline is general. It is not a failing of people who do nothing.

For endurance, the review by Burtscher and colleagues (2022) recalls that VO2max falls by about 10% per decade in healthy sedentary adults, from age 25 to 30, a little more at older ages.1 This figure serves as a benchmark for what follows: it is the “average” slope of a person who does not train.

For performance, let us look at people who train enough to be ranked. Ganse and colleagues analysed 27,088 annual results from the North Rhine-Westphalia athletics rankings (2001 to 2014), across 12 events and athletes aged 11 to 89. They measure the percentage of performance lost each year, relative to performance at age 30. Between 30 and 69, the decline is linear: in men, 0.58% per year in the 100 m, 1.07% in the 400 m, 1.08% in the 800 m and 0.94% in the 5,000 m. Beyond 70, the curve bends downwards in running events.6

In ranked men, the decline is steady up to 69, then accelerates

Percentage of performance (relative to that at age 30) lost per year, men. One single scale for the eight bars. Mostly cross-sectional data: athletes of different ages are compared in the same year. Each age category contains only the best ranked results. Source: Ganse et al., Frontiers in Physiology, 2018.6

What this means

Even among people active enough to be ranked, performance falls every year, by about 1% per year in men between 30 and 69, or 6 to 11% per decade (derived calculation: annual value multiplied by ten). This is of the same order as the 10% of VO2max in sedentary people. Training therefore does not remove the slope. And after 70, the annual loss doubles or triples in these events: it rises to as much as 3% per year in the 800 m and the 5,000 m. The earlier you reach this step with a good base, the more margin you have before it gets in your way.

If everyone declines, including active people, the question becomes: by how much, and depending on what? This is where follow-up studies, which take the same people again over the years, become valuable.

Step 2 of 6 · The groups

The slope is not the same for everyone, and training weighs heavily

The claim: at the same age, those who keep their training load lose markedly less endurance.

The 2022 review brought together six studies that followed the same masters endurance athletes for 6 to 22 years (ages 46.5 to 82.8 at the end of follow-up) and sorted them according to how their training volume changed. For men, three tiers appear: volume maintained or reduced by at most 10%, VO2max decline of 5 to 6.5% per decade; volume reduced by 11 to 20%, decline of 8 to 26%; volume reduced by more than 20% or nearly sedentary, decline of 15 to 46%.1

The more you ease off, the faster VO2max falls

Solid: low end of the range; pale: up to the high end. One single scale for the four bars. The ranges come from small groups (6 to 34 people), mostly men. Source: Burtscher et al., Int J Environ Res Public Health, 2022.1

Two examples from the review show that the gap does not come down to a single group. In the study by Katzel and colleagues, the decline per decade is 6% in highly trained men, 26% in moderately trained men and 36% in untrained men. In Trappe and colleagues, the longest, it is 6%, 11% and 15%. The order is the same.1

The authors also calculated how much of the variation training explains: the change in volume accounts for 54% of the differences in decline in men and 39% in women; with age added, this rises to 70% in men.1 More than half of the differences therefore comes down to what you keep doing; the rest is age, genetics and health.

What this means

Two 50-year-olds at the same level do not end up in the same place at 70, depending on what they do in between. The one who keeps their load loses about half as fast as the reference decline in sedentary people (5 to 6.5% versus about 10%), a comparison valid for men. The one who stops almost everything can lose up to 46% in ten years.

To see what these percentages do over several decades, we can run them over a career. The example below is a calculation, not a measurement: it starts from a chosen value and applies the same decline each decade.

Three slopes, the same starting point: one crosses the independence threshold before 70

Derived figures: 30 mL/kg/min at 50 chosen for the example, then a constant decline of 6%, 10% or 26% per decade (low end of the range for masters who maintain volume, sedentary benchmark, high end of the range for masters whose volume falls by 11 to 20%). In reality the decline is not constant and accelerates with age (step 4). Threshold: Shephard, Br J Sports Med.1,15

What this means

With the sedentary reference slope, this starting level stays above the threshold until 90. With the high end of the range, it crosses it around 67 (calculation). The difference between these lines is years of independence, and that is exactly what is at stake. The example depends on the starting point: a lower starting level brings each curve closer to the threshold.

We now know that the slope varies. We can ask what declines inside the body, and whether everything declines in the same way.

Step 3 of 6 · The mechanisms

What declines in the body, and what holds

The claim: the body's systems do not all age at the same pace, and some respond better than others to training.

The heart. For endurance, the 2022 review identifies the fall in maximal heart rate and in stroke volume (the blood pumped out with each beat) as the main contributors to the loss of VO2max in masters. Even a highly trained athlete has an engine whose maximum revs and displacement decline with age; the exact mechanisms remain poorly understood.1

Muscle. A nine-year retest of masters cyclists sheds light on this point. Milbourn and colleagues re-examined 15 cyclists from the London cohort (14 men and one woman), aged 74 on average at the end, whose cycling volume had not changed: 585 km per month at the start, 570 nine years later.5

Same training volume, but the body changes composition

Derived figures: value after nine years relative to the starting value (for example 50.5 kg out of 54.8 kg of lean mass), rounded. “Significant” comes from the source. 15 people, only one woman. Source: Milbourn et al., conference abstract, Proc Physiol Soc, 2022.5

What this means

Despite stable training, these cyclists lost 8% of lean mass and gained 15% of fat mass, and their peak power fell by 11%. But leg and hand strength, as well as the Timed Up and Go test, did not change in a demonstrated way, and power relative to the remaining muscle holds. The muscle shrinks; what is left keeps working. For you, strength training after 50 is first of all about holding on to what you have.

At the tissue level, Pollock and colleagues took thigh biopsies from 90 of these cyclists (aged 55 to 79, about 26 years of practice on average). They find no link between age and the proportion or size of fibres, nor with mitochondria, except a weak fall in capillary density in men (r = 0.299, about 9% of the variance). Limits given by the authors: no sedentary group to compare with, different ages compared at the same time, very active volunteers.3

Immunity. Duggal and colleagues compared 125 of these cyclists with 75 inactive adults of the same age and 55 young adults. The cyclists have more “naive” T lymphocytes and more cells recently released from the thymus than the inactive people, at a level comparable to that of the young, with more IL-7 (which supports the thymus) and less IL-6 (associated with its atrophy). But “senescent” CD8 T cells do not differ between cyclists and inactive people: activity does not protect against everything.4

Partial conclusion: training slows some losses and not others, and even when very active, you lose muscle. It remains to be seen whether this picture holds in cases that depart from the average: the oldest, women, different sports.

Step 4 of 6 · Special cases

After 70, in women, depending on the event

The claim: the general rule (slow decline, slowed by training) has exceptions and poorly known areas.

After 70. We saw it for men. In ranked women, the values after 70 are even higher: 5.97% per year in the 400 m, 9.63% in the 800 m, 7.89% in the 5,000 m, compared with 1.42%, 1.17% and 0.84% before 70. Caution: these figures rest on very few participants (21 women over 69 in the 200 m, for example), and the authors consider that the differences between sexes are partly due to these numbers.6

Depending on the event. The acceleration is not universal: it is significant in all sprint and running events for both sexes, but not in the long jump, and in the shot put only in men.6 Endurance events are therefore the ones that fall fastest after 70. One could see a link with the fall in stroke volume seen above, a connection the study does not test.

Women and endurance. The 2022 review contains only two studies for women. Examples of VO2max decline per decade: 9% (51 years, volume reduced by 22%), 16% (58 years, volume reduced by 19%), 24% (73 years, volume reduced by 39%). But a group of 61-year-old women whose volume had increased by 20% lost 12%. The authors judge the association weaker in women: volume explains 39% of the differences, compared with 54% in men.1

Swimming and learning. Rubin and colleagues followed 45 masters swimming champions (aged 25 to 96, 23 years of competition on average) and compared them with world records by age. Their individual slopes are gentler than those of the records, which the authors attribute mainly to a learning effect at the start of the masters career: training improves technique at the same time as fitness. Past the peak, their decline joins that of the records.7

What this means

Keep three nuances in mind. The drop after 70 is real for endurance events. Data on women are too scarce to claim that training acts in the same way, even though nothing suggests otherwise. Finally, part of masters' apparent progress comes from learning (technique), not only from physiology: a better performance does not by itself prove a body that ages more slowly.

So far, everything rests on comparisons: groups that train more or less. To know whether training really causes these gaps, we need trials in which people's training is changed and we watch what happens.

Step 5 of 6 · The cause

When training is changed, what happens?

The claim: stopping costs quickly, resuming pays back quickly, and trials show real effects at every age studied, including in sedentary people.

Stopping and resuming. The 2022 review draws on detraining data (Coyle and colleagues, 1984): in seven people aged about 29, VO2max falls by 7% after 12 days of stopping, by 14% after 56 days and by 18% after 84 days. On resuming, VO2max rises by 29.3% in 84 days in 68-year-old men, against 15.4% in 23-year-old men.1

Stopping loses quickly, resuming regains quickly

Change in VO2max. One single scale (10 units of width per percentage point). The stopping data come from a small group of young people; the resumption data, from people who were not masters athletes. Source: Burtscher et al. 2022, citing Coyle (1984) and Murias.1

What this means

The body loses in a few weeks what it took months to build, and regains it quickly when you resume, faster in the older men of the study than in the young ones (the source does not say whether this is because they started from lower). A break of a few weeks (injury, travel) is therefore not a permanent loss.

Trials in people over 60. The test closest to proof is the randomised trial: who trains is decided by lot. The LIFE trial followed 1,635 sedentary people aged 70 to 89, with physical limitations but able to walk 400 m, for 2.6 years on average. One group followed a structured programme of moderate intensity (walking, strength training, flexibility: two sessions at the centre and three to four at home per week), the other health workshops and stretching.13

A structured programme reduces the risk of losing the ability to walk, in a randomised trial

Share of participants affected after 2.6 years on average. Difference in risk of losing the ability to walk: risk ratio 0.82 (95% confidence interval: 0.69 to 0.98); persistent disability: 0.72 (0.57 to 0.91). Serious adverse events: 49.4% versus 45.7% (ratio 1.08; 0.98 to 1.20). Source: Pahor et al., JAMA, 2014 (abstract).13

What this means

In people who were already limited, aged nearly 79 on average, structured activity reduced the risk of losing the ability to walk 400 m by about a fifth, and of losing it persistently by about a quarter. The random allocation rules out the explanation “they were already in better health”. But the activity group had slightly more serious adverse events (a difference not demonstrated: the interval includes 1).

Strength trials confirm this. A Cochrane review of 121 randomised trials and 6,700 older participants finds a large effect on strength (standardised mean difference of 0.84; confidence interval of 0.67 to 1.00) and a walking speed higher by 0.08 m/s (0.04 to 0.12). Adverse events were poorly recorded there; the serious ones, rare, were not linked to the programme. The trial search stops in 2007-2008.9 In the McCartney trial (60 to 80 years, 42 weeks, two sessions per week at 50 to 80% of maximal load), strength rose by up to 65%, the quadriceps by 5.5%, with no change in bone density.10 In nine nursing-home residents of about 90, eight weeks of strength training gave +174% in strength and +48% in walking speed: a tiny sample, but a response exists even at this age.11 Finally, a meta-analysis of 37 studies in healthy people over 60 finds that weight training also improves endurance (+1.89 mL/kg/min of peak VO2, programmes of less than 24 weeks).12

Causation is therefore well established for strength and mobility. It remains to face the objections squarely, and what nobody yet knows.

Step 6 of 6 · The objections

What remains uncertain

Objection 1: masters are a special group. That is correct. The London cyclists had to ride 100 km in under 6 h 30 (men) or 60 km in under 5 h 30 (women), and smokers, heavy drinkers and people with high blood pressure or other diseases were excluded.2 Athletics rankings contain only athletes who keep competing.6 Those who get injured or ill drop out of the samples, which makes the observed slope gentler than that of an ordinary population making the same effort. This is plausible reasoning, not measured by these studies. So the masters' slope cannot be promised to everyone.

Objection 2: causation may run the other way. Stephen Harridge, professor at King's College London, summarises the London cohort this way: these people are healthy because they have trained for a long time, and without the activity their health would probably deteriorate. The press release provides no evidence for this direction of the arrow.2 In the Newcastle 85+ cohort, falling grip strength goes with a higher risk of death, but the authors see it as a sign of deteriorating health, not a cause.16 The same logic applies to training: when someone falls ill, they reduce their volume. Part of the gap observed in step 2 may come from this, without our knowing which part. The randomised trials of step 5 get around the problem, but for strength and mobility, not for mortality.

Objection 3: comparisons of different ages flatter. The 2018 press release claims that these cyclists did not lose muscle mass or muscular strength with age. This conclusion comes from different ages compared at the same time. When the same people are taken again nine years later (step 3), lean mass does fall by 8%.2,5 So beware of phrases such as “exercise stops ageing”.

What we do not know. First, whether starting late lets you catch up with long-time masters: I found no study comparing people who start after 60 with lifelong athletes. Trials show gains in sedentary people, mainly in strength and mobility. Second, how much of the gap comes from genetics: training volume does not explain all of the variation, and we cannot isolate the rest. Finally, effects on mood or memory are not covered in the sources read here, and the article says nothing about them.

The answer to the question

Let us return to the question posed at the start: does training change the speed of decline, and what should you do at your age?

Solid. Decline exists for everyone, athletes included. For strength and the ability to walk, training has a causal effect demonstrated by randomised trials in people aged 60 to 90, including sedentary people, with gains that appear within a few weeks.

Probable. For endurance, keeping your training load goes with a VO2max decline about twice as slow as that of sedentary people in men (5 to 6.5% versus about 10% per decade), and training volume explains more than half of the differences. This is an association observed in small follow-up groups: part of it may come from selection and illness.

Not demonstrated. That any given man or woman gets the masters' slope; that starting at 60 catches up with a lifetime of training; that the effect is the same in women; that training extends lifespan in these data.

So yes, what you do changes the slope, but it does not cancel it: muscle is lost even in the very active, and the drop after 70 mainly affects endurance. And yes, it is still time: what the trials show is that strength and mobility respond at every age studied, including at 90, and that both the loss and the regain of endurance are quick. The most useful thing to remember is this: the realistic goal is not to stay young, it is to reach 80 far from the threshold where independence is lost.

What to put in place

Here is what the sources allow us to recommend, in the order in which I would do it.

  1. Measure your starting point.Do the test on this page with its age norm table, in conditions you can reproduce (same time of day, same warm-up, same place). Without a starting point, you will not know whether your slope changes.
  2. Keep your training load before looking for more.This is the variable that separates a slow decline from a fast one in the 2022 review. If you have to cut back (injury, family), cut by less than 10% rather than stopping: this is the limit of the “volume maintained” tier.
  3. Do two strength sessions per week.This is the WHO minimum, and the McCartney trial obtained its gains this way, at 50 to 80% of maximal load. Aim for the large muscle groups; the first gains arrive within a few weeks.
  4. Add balance from age 65.The WHO recommends multicomponent activities (balance, coordination, functional strength) at least three days per week to reduce falls. This can be done within the strength sessions.
  5. Aim for 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity per week.This is the WHO benchmark for health, not an athlete's programme. If you are preparing for a competition, you will do more.8
  6. Redo the test every three to six months.This interval is a practical choice on my part, not a value taken from a study. Always compare in the same conditions. A single drop does not mean much: look at the trend over several tests.

If you have heart disease, joint pain or heavy medication, talk to your doctor before increasing intensity. In the LIFE trial, serious events were slightly more frequent in the active group: medical advice is not a formality.13,9

Limits of this article
  • The follow-up studies are small: 6 to 34 people per subgroup in the review, 15 cyclists in the nine-year retest (conference abstract), mostly men.1,5
  • Several trials are old (1990, 1995, Cochrane search stopped in 2008), and the threshold of 18 and 15 mL/kg/min comes from a single-author review, with approximate ages.9,10,15

Frequently asked questions

Does training prevent decline?

No, it slows it. Even those who keep their volume lose VO2max and muscle.1,5

Do you need to have been athletic all your life?

Studies of masters athletes do not answer this question. The LIFE trial and the strength trials show gains in sedentary older people, without our knowing whether they catch up with those of a lifetime of training.10,13

Are women different?

We do not know well: few studies, and only one woman in the nine-year retest. In the 2022 review, the association between training volume and decline is weaker in women.1,5

What if I stop for a few weeks?

You lose quickly (7% of VO2max after 12 days in a small study of young people), but you regain quickly on resuming.1
